angle: A doctor who pays life for everything and bills it back through nine drains: six verified kill shapes whose BOUNDS are the piloting lesson — two unbounded loops you decide on once, one mandatory loop that wins because it cannot stop, two library-bounded lines you count at the table, and a primary engine that kills in installments — flown by trading the commander freely in the grind and protecting him absolutely on the engine turn, with the one honest hole, zero artifact answers, played as politics.

cover.dominant_coverline: SIX WAYS TO END A TABLE
teases: Stack 011: the loop that costs nothing, and you finish at 80 life
Stack 012 cannot stop — and that is why it wins instead of drawing
The undying pair, counted: lethal at ~30 of the ~55 activations your library permits
Zero artifact answers in all 80 entries. The politics that buys you somebody else's.

departments.headline: TRADE HIM. THEN PROTECT HIM.
departments.dek: One card in this deck is exempt from variance, and a single rule says so. Three of your six verified kills need him standing and the other three never say his name — so when do you spend the guarantee, and when do you spend the insurance?
departments.body:
Begin with the clause that makes this format unlike every other one. CR 903.8: "A player may cast a commander they own from the command zone." Yawgmoth is therefore not a card you draw. He is a card you have. The simulation casts him in 9,850 of 10,000 games, mean turn 4.301, median 4, and 7,188 of those land him on turn four exactly — 91% are on the battlefield by turn six, and the 718 turn-two arrivals every one ride Sol Ring, Ancient Tomb or Dark Ritual.

The price of the guarantee sits in the same rule, and it compounds: "an additional {2} for each previous time the player casting it has cast it from the command zone that game." Four mana, then six, then eight, then ten. Set that schedule beside mean available mana of 3.908 on turn four, 5.230 on turn six and 7.104 on turn ten. The holding is short: the first recast costs you a turn, and the third costs a turn nobody at this table is going to give you. Notice, though, which of your saves are not recasts at all — Malakir Rebirth and Supernatural Stamina return him to the battlefield or keep him there, so the tax never advances.

Colour identity is CR 903.4 — "the color or colors of any mana symbols in that card's mana cost or rules text". One black symbol in his cost, one colour in the deck, and the mana audit has nothing to reconcile: black is 100% of the pip load and 100% of the sources, on curve at 94.8% once the rocks and dorks are counted. What that identity costs is breadth, and this issue keeps the bill in view: no counterspell, and not one card among all 80 entries that destroys or exiles an artifact. Five tutors cannot find what is not there.

Commander damage the record disposes of quickly. CR 903.10a removes a player dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander. Yawgmoth is a 2/4 who would much rather be sacrificing than attacking; 21 damage is eleven connections. A coincidence here, never a clock.

Now the clause to memorise, because it cuts both ways. CR 702.16b: a permanent with protection cannot be targeted by abilities from a source with the stated quality. Yawgmoth is a Human with protection from Humans, so his own ability can never target him — the 2/4 who could comfortably absorb counters is not allowed to take one. The Counselor's files lean on this: once an opponent's creature is gone, every legal target is one of your own bodies, which is exactly what bounds a Nest rotation at five to eight activations. In the other direction it is free armour at a table thick with Human commanders.

One last fact about the zone: four players can see it, and they cannot see your hand. What the table prices when this commander resolves is a reputation. The bracket sheet agrees with them — floor 4, Optimized, forced independently by four Game Changers and by eleven two-card infinite records, inside a declared target of 4.

COACH'S READ. The rule is phase, not posture. Three of your six signed kills never name him — both Gravecrawler loops and the Exquisite Blood pair. Three gate on him, including the primary Nest engine and both counted undying lines. So in the grind, trade him cheerfully: he is a draw engine and a removal magnet, the recast is two mana and a turn, and removal spent on him is removal not spent on your drains. On the engine turn he is the hub, and exactly three cards can carry him through a removal spell — Lightning Greaves, Supernatural Stamina, Malakir Rebirth. Those are engine-turn cards. Never spend one for value, and never mulligan toward a commander who arrives on his own in seven games of ten.

captions.Malakir Rebirth // Malakir Mire: **A RESCUE IS NOT A RECAST:** it returns him to the battlefield, so the commander tax never advances — and the return is one more death trigger for every drain you have down.
captions.Lightning Greaves: **INSURANCE, NOT ARMOUR:** equip is sorcery speed, so the turn to arm him is the turn before you need him. Shroud cuts you off from your own tricks too — move the boots before you target him yourself.

pilot_tips.text: The best reason to keep him on the battlefield is this card — free removal that exiles, on any turn you spent assembling.

departments.headline: A VALUE DECK UNTIL IT ISN'T
departments.dek: The table sees a swarm of one-mana bodies and a doctor drawing cards. What they are looking at is six verified ways to end all of them at once — you just haven't picked one yet.

callouts.title: BUY CHEAP, BUY EARLY
callouts.text: Your enabler classes arrive first and they arrive on their own: renewable fodder at a mean draw turn of 2.578, a drain at 2.582, a free repeatable outlet at 2.690, an ignition source at 2.818. Carrion Feeder, Viscera Seer, Fume Spitter, Bitterblossom and Reassembling Skeleton all cost one or two mana. Put them down and stop admiring them.

callouts.title: LAND HIM ON CURVE, THEN DIG
callouts.text: The commander lands on turn four in 7,188 of 10,000 goldfished games and is on the battlefield by turn six in 91%. From that turn every spare body is a card, at no mana, at instant speed, on other people's turns. One honest note about every number in this issue: the goldfish does not model his draw, so each unassisted rate is a floor on games where he sticks and digs.

callouts.title: HOLD THE DRAIN
callouts.text: You hold some drain by turn ten in 82.3% of games, and by turn six in 72.0%. Bastion of Remembrance specifically — the drain five signed files resolved with — is one card at 17.8%. It is the piece that reveals the plan, so it goes down last, at the end step before your own turn.

callouts.title: NAME THE SHAPE BEFORE YOU GO
callouts.text: Six shapes, and you name yours before you commit: two unbounded loops, one mandatory pair that cannot stop, two library-bounded lines you count at the table, and the primary — Nest of Scarabs plus any of nine drains, killing in installments. Every one ends all opponents at the same check, so never aim a kill at a seat. Ask which shape you are one card away from.

captions.Yawgmoth, Thran Physician: **THE DRAW ENGINE:** 'Pay 1 life, Sacrifice another creature' has no mana anywhere in it, so no tax and no Sphere reaches it. Use him to draw for three or four turns before you use him for anything else.
captions.Gravecrawler: **THE HUB IN FURNITURE'S CLOTHES:** a one-mana 2/1 that cannot block, in a deck full of them — and the recursive half of both unbounded kills. Nobody spends removal on it. Deploy it turn one.
captions.Bastion of Remembrance: **THE PAYOFF THAT LOOPS:** the drain in five of the eleven signed files, and an enchantment — your own engine can never eat it and a wrath never touches it.

pilot_tips.text: Play it on turn one and let the table file it as a body — the tell in this deck is never Gravecrawler, it is whatever you play beside it.
Cast it on turn two every single time — a body every upkeep for 1 life is the cheapest fodder you will ever buy.

departments.pull_quote: You are nothing, and then you are the whole table. There is no board in between.

departments.headline: ELEVEN GROUPS, AND THE ONE THAT ISN'T HERE
departments.dek: Read the first group and you know how this deck ends games. Read to the end and you will notice the group nobody could write for it: the cards that destroy an artifact.

roster.role: The six kills — the cards that end the table
The other drains — each opponent, or one
Free sacrifice outlets — 78.5% by turn ten
Renewable fodder — the bodies that come back
Mana that is not a land

callouts.title: TWO CARDS CARRY THE LOOPS
callouts.text: Gravecrawler is the recursive half of both unbounded kills; Bastion of Remembrance is the drain five signed files resolved with. Each is one card, about 7% of an opening seven, drawn by turn ten in 17.0% and 17.8% of games unassisted. Five tutors are the only redundancy either of them has — and the record shows no substitute exists for the Crawler in the format's colour.

callouts.title: EACH OPPONENT, OR TARGET PLAYER
callouts.text: On the identical grinding board, a drain reading 'each opponent' bills every seat at once. Blood Artist, which reads 'target player loses 1 life', removed eight life of a pod's 160. Sort your drains by that word before you sort them by anything else.

callouts.title: THE GROUP WITH NO CARDS IN IT
callouts.text: Feed the Swarm is the only entry in the 99 that destroys a noncreature permanent an opponent controls, and it reads creature or enchantment. Across all 80 entries' oracle text, artifact answers come to zero and land answers to zero. The recursion suite wants your own graveyard intact, and the cheapest permanent that seals a graveyard is an artifact.

callouts.title: TWO CARDS THE TAXONOMY CANNOT SEE
callouts.text: Role coverage is 97.5%, and the two it misses are Plumb the Forbidden and Supernatural Stamina — the instant-speed answer to a wrath, and a two-mana trick that both saves the commander and hands you a death trigger. Absence of a role is not absence of the function. Read the card.

captions.Nest of Scarabs: **SETTLED ARITHMETIC:** count by creatures touched, not counters placed — one proliferate across three counter-bearing creatures makes three Insects, not six. The primary engine's piece, and a one-of with no substitute.
captions.Ophiomancer: **A BODY PER UPKEEP, EVERY UPKEEP:** a deathtouch Snake at the start of each upkeep, yours and theirs, so long as the last one is gone. Feed each Snake to an outlet before the next upkeep and one two-drop pays the commander forever.
captions.Jet Medallion: **A DISCOUNT IS NOT A SOURCE:** one generic off every black spell you cast, which plays a spell deeper most turns. It never appears in the source column, and the commander's ability was already free.

pilot_tips.text: Use it for outlet work and bulk mana only — its colorless does not pay Gravecrawler's {B}.

departments.pull_quote: Thirty-nine combo lines are fully contained in this list, eleven of them two-card infinites. Eight signed files make six of them shapes. Containment is a shortlist, never evidence.

departments.headline: SHAPE, NOT NAMES
departments.dek: You keep the first seven 81.6% of the time at a mean of 0.222 mulligans, so the deck is not asking you to gamble. The question is never whether the commander is here — it is whether the hand makes bodies and can spend one for free.

hands.why: Three lands is the modal kept hand — 3,561 of 10,000 keeps hold exactly three. This one already carries a free outlet, renewable fodder, an ignition source and an each-opponent drain: the four classes the model finds earliest, at mean draw turns of 2.690, 2.578, 2.818 and 2.582. Nothing in it costs more than two.

Fast mana is the thinnest class on the sheet — three cards, 43.6% by turn ten — and 718 of 10,000 games cast the commander on turn two, every one off exactly this. The Skeleton gives him something to eat the moment he lands, and a tutor is what carries the fastest kill from 6.6% to 42.6%.

All payoff, nothing underneath it. Mean available mana is 3.908 on turn four and 4.606 on turn five, so a six-drop and two five-drops with no enabler in front of them means you do nothing for half the game. Enablers dig toward payoffs. Payoffs sit there waiting for an engine nobody built.

This is a kill in your hand and it is still a ship. One land — 1,429 of 10,000 first sevens hold exactly one, and one land is a mulligan unless Sol Ring, Ancient Tomb or Dark Ritual sits beside it. The second Zombie the Altar loop needs is not here either. Ship it and you will draw into a shape; keep it and you will watch one.

captions.Dark Ritual: **ONE BLACK INTO THREE, ONCE:** a ritual is not a source and the audit never counts it as one. It buys a specific turn — a turn-one Bitterblossom, a turn-two commander — so spend it on the turn that changes the game.
captions.Skullclamp: **KEEPABLE ON ITS OWN:** one mana, and every 1/1 you make becomes two cards. It is the draw engine that still works on the turns your commander is answered.

pilot_tips.text: Never ship a hand for lacking him — he arrives on turn four in 7,188 of 10,000 games without any help from you.

departments.pull_quote: Two to five lands, something that sacrifices, something to sacrifice. Only 284 first sevens in 10,000 come out landless — the hard decision almost never arrives.

departments.headline: PICK BEFORE YOU READ
departments.dek: One board hands you six mana, a running engine and no kill. The other hands you a one-mana artifact you cannot break — four branches each, and you commit out loud before the Coach shows his hand.
departments.pull_quote: Stop asking which payoff is biggest. Ask which one is still on the battlefield next turn.
departments.note: EDITOR: both spreads render from decisions/ (001 what-the-six-mana-buys, 002 the-cage-you-cannot-break) and both boards are drawn from the current 99. Furniture above deliberately quotes no kill counts and names no recommended branch — decision 002's own title states a kill count in its own words, so nothing here repeats or contradicts it.

departments.headline: SIX SHAPES, SIX BOUNDS
departments.dek: Eleven case files, six kills. Two run forever, one wins because it cannot stop, two you count against your own library, and the one you will play most is a pace.

callouts.title: THE PRIMARY IS A PACE
callouts.text: Nest of Scarabs plus any of nine drains, Yawgmoth working from the zone — files 002, 003 and 004. One rotation is bounded by its own bodies at five to eight activations, roughly two drains per body, and protection from Humans is why it stops: he cannot target himself, so once the opponent's creature is gone every legal target is one of your own tokens. The kill is rotations stacked across turns — the table's life falls in installments, and by turn six the pieces are together in 7.5% of games on your own draws, 38.9% with a wish.

callouts.title: UNBOUNDED: IT FUNDS ITSELF
callouts.text: Warren Soultrader, Gravecrawler, Bastion of Remembrance — file 009. Gravecrawler's ability modifies the zone its own card may be cast from, so the permission is live in the graveyard every iteration, the Zombie condition held by Soultrader — whom 'another creature' keeps out of the loop forever. Each activation's Treasure exactly funds the next cast, your life nets zero, and each opponent pays one per lap for as long as you care to lap.

callouts.title: UNBOUNDED: IT PAYS YOU
callouts.text: Swap the Treasure for Phyrexian Altar, with Carrion Feeder holding the Zombie condition and never the sacrifice — file 011. The Altar's ability needs no target and could add mana, so it is a mana ability that never uses the stack: the {B} is in your pool before anyone receives priority. Each lap gains you a life, the board returns to an identical state, and you finish the game at 80.

callouts.title: MANDATORY, AND NOT A DRAW
callouts.text: Exquisite Blood beside a body reading 'Whenever you gain life, each opponent loses 1 life' — file 012. Neither card says 'may', so the loop is compulsory, and it still does not force a draw: a draw needs a sequence that could be repeated indefinitely, and every cycle here lowers every opponent's life, so there is a way to stop. Drain 40 takes all opponents from 1 to 0 at one state-based check, and the only player left is you.

callouts.title: COUNTED: 39 AGAINST 59
callouts.text: Mikaeus grants undying, and your commander's -1/-1 counter does not shrink the returned body: it annihilates the +1/+1 undying left behind and re-arms the creature to die again — file 010. But the commander's draw has no 'may', so your library is the clock: 39 further activations needed against the 59 it permits, a margin of 20.

callouts.title: COUNTED: 30 AGAINST 55
callouts.text: Butcher Ghoul and Geralf's Messenger alternating under Yawgmoth, a drain down — file 014. The alternation is genuine: each undying return leaves a +1/+1, the commander's counter strips it by state-based action, and the body dies counter-free again — 'unbounded' is refuted only because every activation is a mandatory draw against a library of roughly 55. The bound never saves the table: each two-activation cycle takes 2 from every opponent and 4 from the Messenger's seat at net-zero life to you, so about 30 activations end the pod with roughly 25 draws of margin.

callouts.title: ONE WORD, AND THE POD SURVIVES
callouts.text: Blood Artist reads 'target player loses 1 life' where the closers read each opponent — file 004. On the identical grinding board: eight triggers, eight life removed of a pod's 160, the arithmetic divided by four with an exhaustive search finding nothing better. Refuted as a kill, and not narrowly — reach and wrath insurance, never the finish.

callouts.title: THREE EDGES FOR THE ROAD
callouts.text: File 005: an Insect killed by its own counter dies at toughness 0, and gaining zero is not gaining — a lifegain-metered drain sees nothing. File 006: a creature that enters already wearing a -1/-1 counter does trigger Nest of Scarabs, because a reference to putting counters covers counters it enters with. File 008: a cost is paid while the ability is already on the stack, so one activation paid with a token pays a create-or-sacrifice drain twice.

captions.Phyrexian Altar: **IT NEVER USES THE STACK:** a mana ability resolves on activation, so the {B} that recasts Gravecrawler is in your pool before anyone can respond. That is what makes file 011 free and uncounterable.
captions.South Wind Avatar: **FOUR TOUGHNESS, FOUR MORE ACTIVATIONS:** on the engine boards its size buys the extra laps a 1/1 drainer cannot. And a token that dies at toughness 0 gains you nothing — so it drains nobody.
captions.Geralf's Messenger: **THE SEAT THAT PAYS DOUBLE:** his enters-trigger bills one chosen opponent 2 on every return, so the pair's cycle costs that seat 4 while the rest pay 2. Aim it at whoever is closest to dead.

pilot_tips.text: Keep her out of the undying loops and save her for the finish — her sacrifice places no counter, and only your commander's counter re-arms a returned body.

departments.pull_quote: An unbounded loop is a decision. A counted loop is arithmetic. The engine is a pace. Know which one you are announcing before you go.

departments.headline: NOTHING, THEN EVERYTHING
departments.dek: There is no board where you are lethal on one seat and merely scary to the rest — every signed shape ends the table together. So what do three opponents actually read off your permanents, and how do you spend the misread?

callouts.title: THREAT WINDOW: THE SHAPE, NOT THE SWARM
callouts.text: The table counts creatures, and the goldfish has you at a mean of 4.239 bodies by turn six — a fair little swarm, and not the plan. The board that ends the game is two to four specific permanents, and nobody at a Commander table audits permanents for a shape. Let them count.

callouts.title: THREAT WINDOW: THE SECOND NONCREATURE PAYOFF
callouts.text: The flip is not board width — it is the second noncreature payoff resolving: Exquisite Blood, an Altar beside a Gravecrawler, Mikaeus untapping. Quiet combo decks are exactly who experienced tables hit, so never claim you have nothing: claim the board they can see — the swarm, the drains — and sell that as the whole story. Then sequence the loud half last, with the table's open mana counted first.

callouts.title: THE PERMANENT YOU CANNOT BUY BACK
callouts.text: Grafdigger's Cage sits on the graveyard-casting and undying halves of the suite on a straight oracle reading; Cursed Totem sits on the creature outlets and the commander himself. Nothing in all 80 entries destroys an artifact, so stop shopping for the answer you do not own. Find the artifact-removal seats at Rule 0, invest early — your spot removal on their problems, your silence on their engines — and the day a Cage resolves, their Disenchant is worth more than any card you draw, so overpay for it.

callouts.title: SAY IT STRAIGHT AT RULE ZERO
callouts.text: Bracket floor 4, Optimized, forced twice over: four Game Changers — Ancient Tomb, Demonic Tutor, Necropotence, Vampiric Tutor — and eleven two-card infinite records, inside a declared target of 4. Then the sentence that matters: six rules-verified kill shapes, two unbounded, every one ending all opponents at once. You never present lethal to a seat, only to the table.

captions.Grave Pact: **THE ROOM-CHANGER:** a drain takes life quietly; an edict takes a creature from every opponent in front of everybody, each time a body of yours dies. Expect to be priced on the edicts, not the drains.
captions.Exquisite Blood: **IT DOES NOTHING THE TURN IT LANDS:** which is exactly why it resolves. Deploy the lifegain body first — a two-mana cleric reads as fair — and let the enchantment look like a lifegain card.
captions.Necropotence: **WHAT ACTUALLY SPENDS YOUR LIFE:** not the engine. This, Bitterblossom, Black Market Connections, City of Brass, Ancient Tomb. One signed loop finishes you at 80 and another nets exactly zero — spend early points like the cheap currency they are.

pilot_tips.text: Equip at sorcery speed the turn before the engine turn — after the removal is announced it is decoration.

departments.pull_quote: You get no warning turn, so neither does the table. Reveal the loud half at the end step before your own.

departments.headline: WHO ACTUALLY BEATS YOU
departments.dek: It is not the wrath — the wrath pays you four different ways. It is a one-mana artifact, so read every box below for the same thing: which of the six shapes does this seat leave alive?

threats.read: Be visibly happy here. Nine drains bill the table when your creatures die, so their sweeper pays you for every body it takes, and your rebuild is structural: Reassembling Skeleton returns for two forever, Gravecrawler for one, Bitterblossom and Ophiomancer produce a body every upkeep without spending a card. Hold two mana whenever the control seat untaps with four or more, and let Plumb the Forbidden turn their announcement into your draw step. The real exposure sits one permanent type higher: every signed kill is a pile of permanents whose noncreature halves — Bastion, the Altar, the Blood — your three protection effects cannot save. Keep the noncreature half in hand until the turn it converts.

This is the seat that actually beats you, and it costs them almost nothing. On a straight oracle reading a Grafdigger's Cage blanks the Gravecrawler recasts under both unbounded loops and every undying return; a Cursed Totem takes the commander's ability and every creature outlet you own. Nothing in the 99 answers either — so do not go shopping. Learn which shapes play through: the Nest engine runs on freshly created tokens, Exquisite Blood touches no graveyard, and under a Totem the noncreature outlets — both Altars and Blasting Station — are the remainder, unverified as a full assembly and honestly a lifeline rather than a plan. Pivot the same turn and aim the next tutor at the surviving shape.

Recount your hand under a tax, never your board — this deck's best property there is verified, not vibes. The commander's ability costs no mana at all. File 009's Treasure exactly funds the next cast, file 011's Altar refunds its own black through a mana ability, file 012's loop is mandatory and spends nothing, file 014 nets zero life per cycle, and Jet Medallion rebates the first mana of every black spell before they even charge it. A Sphere halves everyone else's turn and does nothing to a loop already running. Your window of weakness is deployment, so deploy each piece the turn you can — the cleaner sequence is not coming.

You are the control seat and the sweepers need no apology: all three — Black Sun's Zenith, Soul Snuffers, The Meathook Massacre — double as engine ignition, because you are the one placing the counters, so no wipe slot is ever dead. An opposing small creature is not even a threat: the engine files establish that a two-toughness enemy body EXTENDS a Nest rotation by two activations, so point the commander's counters outward whenever a legal target exists and say thank you. Spend life freely early — one signed loop refunds you to 80 — and switch from spending to defending one turn before it matters, not one after.

Your hardest seat, so play it with your whole chest. You cannot interact on the stack at all — every answer you hold points at a permanent — so held answers rot: spend removal on the enabler the turn it lands. Deadly Rollick is free while your commander is out, which is most turns from four on. Then race with the shape you can finish, not the one you prefer: Exquisite Blood assembles earliest at a mean turn of 5.085 and hits 42.6% with a tutor behind it, and the commander's outlet works at instant speed once the permanents are down. One caution from the record: file 012's board ignited from South Wind Avatar's own dies-trigger lifegain — Marauding Blight-Priest and Starscape Cleric carry the drain text but gain no life themselves, so line up the first lifegain event before you count on either.

It earns its own box because it splits your kill suite cleanly in half on a straight oracle reading: the Gravecrawler loops cast out of the graveyard every lap, and both counted lines return creatures through it — four of six shapes look Cage-shaped — while the Nest engine runs on freshly created tokens and Exquisite Blood never touches a graveyard at all. Nothing signed settles that split, so hold it as a working read: under hate, abandon recursion on the spot and tutor toward the engine (38.9% by turn six, assisted) or the Blood (fastest, mean 5.085). You hate back with one land: Bojuka Bog exiles a graveyard on an uncounted land drop.

captions.Plumb the Forbidden: **THE WRATH, CONVERTED:** sacrifice any number of creatures as an additional cost and copy it for each — their announcement becomes your draw step, and every death fires whatever drain you have down.
captions.Feed the Swarm: **THE WHOLE ANSWER TO A CLASS:** the only card in the 99 that destroys a noncreature permanent an opponent controls, and it reads creature or enchantment. A resolved artifact has no answer in this library.

pilot_tips.text: Bank it — it enters tapped anyway, so play it on the turn their graveyard matters rather than the turn it is convenient.

departments.pull_quote: Interaction slots are the price of a linear engine. You paid it, and the bill arrives as a two-mana artifact you cannot remove.

departments.headline: WISH FOR THE KILL, NOT THE ENGINE
departments.dek: Your enabler classes turn up on their own in four games of five. Your kills do not — so what is a tutor actually buying, and which single card completes two of them?

callouts.title: NEVER WISH FOR A COVERED CLASS
callouts.text: By turn ten, on your own draws: a drain 82.3%, renewable fodder 82.3%, a free repeatable outlet 78.5%, an ignition source 73.8%. Those cards are already coming. The one engine errand a wish is allowed to run is fast mana — three cards, 43.6%, the smallest and lowest-rated class on the sheet.

callouts.title: THE KILLS ARE WHAT MOVES
callouts.text: The Nest engine goes 7.5% to 38.9% assembled by turn six. Exquisite Blood 6.6% to 42.6% overall — the biggest mover on the sheet. The Mikaeus line 4.6% to 34.3%, the undying pair 1.8% to 26.9%, the Soultrader loop 1.3% to 18.2%, the Altar loop 0.6% to 12.0% — multiples every one, and that is the entire job of these five cards.

callouts.title: THE DEFAULT FETCH IS NEST OF SCARABS
callouts.text: The primary line runs through one card with no substitute in the colour, and these five tutors are its only redundancy — demand a reason to deviate. When you do: Gravecrawler completes both unbounded kills at once (17.0% on your own draws), and Bastion of Remembrance is the drain five signed files resolved with (17.8%). A wish on either is a wish on several kills.

callouts.title: KNOW YOUR OWN CAPS
callouts.text: Beseech the Mirror's bargained free cast stops at mana value 4: it reaches Nest of Scarabs, Bastion of Remembrance, Warren Soultrader, Phyrexian Altar, Marauding Blight-Priest, Starscape Cleric, South Wind Avatar and Feed the Swarm — and never Exquisite Blood at 5 or Mikaeus at 6. Those two belong to Demonic Tutor. Vampiric Tutor lands on top and costs the draw step, so book it at the end step before your own turn.

captions.Diabolic Intent: **THE COST THAT ISN'T:** the creature you sacrifice is a drain trigger with any payoff down, an edict with Grave Pact, and a Spawn with Pawn of Ulamog out. Pay it with a token, never with a piece.
captions.Demonic Tutor: **NO CONDITIONS, NO CEILING:** the only wish that does not care what the card costs, which makes it the only route to Exquisite Blood or Mikaeus on curve.
captions.Vampiric Tutor: **AN APPOINTMENT, NOT AN ARRIVAL:** it books the card on top for two life, so the transit turn is the price. Fire it at the end step before your own and the price rounds to nothing.

pilot_tips.text: Cast both Spree modes and point the draw at yourself — the search resolves first, so the draw delivers exactly what you just booked.

departments.pull_quote: You are not tutoring to make this deck function. You are tutoring to convert.

departments.headline: ONE COLOUR, NOTHING TO RECONCILE
departments.dek: Pip share and source share cannot disagree when there is only one colour to be short of, so the audit narrows to a single number — and the yardstick it is measured against is not reachable in a deck built like this one. Here is what the gap actually costs: almost nothing.

callouts.title: THE YARDSTICK YOU CANNOT HIT
callouts.text: The model wants 36 black sources for a 90% on-curve rate. The lands supply 33 — the whole gap is the three that make no counted black: Ancient Tomb taps for {C}{C}, Urborg taps for nothing on its own, and Nykthos gets no unconditional credit because devotion is exactly the restriction the counter refuses to price. Lands alone: 86.9% on curve, and the audit says it plainly — the target is a yardstick, not a possibility, in a 36-land deck.

callouts.title: EIGHT PRODUCERS CLOSE IT
callouts.text: Ten nonland cards produce mana and eight add black — Agadeem's Awakening, Dark Ritual, Deadly Dispute, Malakir Rebirth, Pawn of Ulamog, Phyrexian Altar, Pitiless Plunderer, Warren Soultrader — lifting 33 to 41 sources and on-curve black to 94.8%. Not one of the eight does it unconditionally: rituals are one-shots, and the rest want a creature to die first, which in this deck is less of a caveat than it sounds. Restricted mana anywhere in the 99: none.

callouts.title: ENGINE MANA IS NOT FAST MANA
callouts.text: Five cards turn a creature death into castable black — 61.2% by turn ten — and that is what makes a sacrifice loop mana-positive rather than merely free. Fast mana is a different resource: Sol Ring, Ancient Tomb, Dark Ritual, 43.6%, the class that buys the turn-two commander. The deck's mana is engine-shaped, not acceleration-shaped, and the two classes buy different turns.

callouts.title: THREE LANDS THE COUNT TREATS ODDLY
callouts.text: Urborg produces nothing and counts for zero sources while making every land on the battlefield a Swamp. Nykthos counts for zero too and pays your devotion to black in a list carrying 76 black pips. Cabal Coffers counts as exactly one source and taps for {B} per Swamp beside 21 basics — one source, zero and zero is the accounting, not the experience.

captions.Swamp: **TWENTY-ONE OF THEM:** the untapped backbone, and the multiplier under Cabal Coffers and Urborg. In mono-black the basic is quietly one of the best cards in the deck.
captions.Phyrexian Tower: **A LAND THAT SACRIFICES:** a free outlet that makes {B}{B} while it does it. Where a spare body is a resource, this is the best untapped land you can draw — once a turn, so pick the turn.

pilot_tips.text: Play it before Cabal Coffers, not after — every land you already control becomes a Swamp the Coffers can count.

departments.pull_quote: Seventy-six black pips across 55 cards, at most three in one cost — and the first is demanded on turn one. Development answers: 99.7% on-time on turn two, 91.6% on turn three.

departments.headline: THE ENGINE ARRIVES. THE KILL IS FETCHED.
departments.dek: Ten thousand openings, seed 42, no opponents and no interaction. The gap between the enabler bars and the kill bars is this deck's whole personality — and there is one number this page refuses to print.

callouts.title: READ EVERY BAR AS A PAIR
callouts.text: The first figure excludes tutors entirely; the second lets one drawn, affordable tutor fill a single missing group. By turn ten: a drain 82.3% / 93.6%, renewable fodder 82.3% / 93.3%, a free repeatable outlet 78.5% / 92.5%, an ignition source 73.8% / 90.2%, engine mana 61.2% / 85.8%. A tutor itself: 61.2%, and it cannot assist its own arrival.

callouts.title: SIX KILLS, SIX NUMBERS
callouts.text: The Nest engine 13.5% / 58.8% assembled, mean turn 6.267 — the deck's best-measured line by a wide margin. Exquisite Blood 6.6% / 42.6% and fastest at a mean of 5.085, Mikaeus 4.6% / 34.3%, the undying pair 1.8% / 26.9%, the Soultrader loop 1.3% / 18.2%, the Altar loop 0.6% / 12.0%. Several rest on one named card, and a named card is about 7% of an opening seven.

callouts.title: THE NUMBER THAT DOES NOT EXIST
callouts.text: There is no union. The simulator scores each requirement group on its own, so a hand holding Exquisite Blood, Gravecrawler and Zulaport Cutthroat satisfies three groups while assembling no kill at all. Nothing on this sheet means 'any kill assembled', we will not compute one, and you should not add these six together either — the shapes share pieces, so the sum double-counts.

callouts.title: THE COMMANDER'S HISTOGRAM
callouts.text: Turn four in 7,188 games of 10,000, mean 4.301, median 4, on the battlefield by turn six in 91%. Turn two happens 718 times, every one off the three-card fast-mana class. He never arrives at all in 150.

callouts.title: THE BAR THAT NAMES THE PROBLEM
callouts.text: An answer to a noncreature permanent, drawn by turn ten: 17.1% — one card, Feed the Swarm, reaching creature or enchantment only, and 67.1% costs a wish that was supposed to buy a kill half. Every other bar measures how well the engine turns up. This one measures what happens when somebody turns it off.

callouts.title: WHAT THE SIMULATION IS NOT
callouts.text: It models resource development, not games: no opponents, no removal, no politics, and a group counts as assembled the moment its cards are drawn. Cost reducers, rituals and extra card draw are not modeled — which means the commander's own mandatory draw, the deck's real selection engine, sits outside every rate quoted. Read the unassisted figures as floors, never predictions.

departments.pull_quote: Six kills. Six numbers. Adding them up would be the only lie in this issue.

departments.headline: ANSWERS FIRST, THEN AMBITION
departments.dek: The first two close measured holes — the artifact zero and the smallest engine class. Seven more extend architecture the case files already signed, and the tenth closes nothing at all and says so on the page.

callouts.title: THE AXIS THAT ACTUALLY BINDS
callouts.text: Interaction-breadth reads 2 of 5 classes, and the artifact class is zero by enumeration of all 80 entries' oracle text — in a format whose cheap hosers for exactly this deck are artifacts. Gate to Phyrexia is the one card on the list that moves the count, 2 to 3, and it is an enchantment, so the Totem it answers cannot switch it off.

callouts.title: THE SMALLEST CLASS ON THE SHEET
callouts.text: Fast mana is three cards at 43.6% — the reason the commander lands on turn two in only 7.2% of sims. Culling the Weak converts a body the deck draws in 82.3% of games into BBBB for one mana. Its cost is stated, not hidden: the ramp count goes one over its window.

callouts.title: NOT ONE LINE HERE IS SIGNED
callouts.text: Every combo a pick would open carries 'needs a stack scenario' by construction. Two are worth a resolve run before any purchase: Bloodthirsty Conqueror beside the three lifegain drains already sleeved, because the whole case is that it doubles Exquisite Blood's scarce half; and Walking Ballista with Mikaeus, because that pick is bought entirely on a line nobody has put through the checker.

callouts.title: HONEST LAST PLACE
callouts.text: Deathgreeter closes nothing any counted axis names, and its entry says so out loud — it holds a slot because roughly half the commander's community lists run it, and the strongest thing a ranked page can do with a famous card the measures cannot see is say exactly that. The floor was recomputed on all ten: bracket 4 before, 4 after, every time.

captions.Feed the Swarm: **THE CARD THE WHOLE PAGE IS ABOUT:** one sorcery, creature or enchantment, and it is the deck's entire answer to a noncreature permanent. Everything ranked here is measured against how much of that gap it closes.

departments.pull_quote: Ten candidates, one recomputed floor: bracket 4 before and after, on all ten. Nothing on this page changes the Rule 0 conversation.

departments.headline: ELEVEN FILES, EVERY QUOTE VERBATIM
departments.dek: Eleven complete resolutions, the checker's verdict as case status, every citation reproduced exactly as the Comprehensive Rules prints it. You do not have to believe this magazine — you can read the record.
departments.pull_quote: Eight of these eleven files carry a kill. The other three settle what a board actually does before you bet a game on it.

departments.headline: SIXTY-EIGHT HANDS, NO HEADLINER
departments.dek: Eighty cards, sixty-eight signatures, and the deepest credit in the book is three. Nobody owns this deck's look — which is itself the story, and it was counted, not felt.

featured.note:
Start with the number that decides this section. Eighty cards counted, sixty-eight different signatures, and no artist painted more than three. There is no standout in this deck, so nobody is going to be told they are one.

Daniel Ljunggren holds the deepest credit at exactly three, and the trio is worth stopping on: Black Sun's Zenith, Jet Medallion, Skullclamp. All three are the deck's rare noncreature tools — the only sweeper whose counters the Nest can read, the discount that plays every black turn one spell deeper, and the one-mana engine that turns each 1/1 into two cards. One hand, three cards, and not a creature among them in a list that runs thirty.

One figure needs saying out loud, because it is the one that lies. Jorge Jacinto's Swamp appears 21 times here and counts once. Authorship is per card, never per copy — count it the other way and a basic land wins this section every single issue. Copies across the whole deck: 100.

The printings cluster where recent Commander cardboard comes from: eleven cards from Lorwyn Eclipsed Commander, ten from Secrets of Strixhaven Commander, seven from Tarkir: Dragonstorm Commander, five from Commander Masters. The analysis reports no contiguous collector-number run anywhere, so nothing here landed as an unopened product — this is breadth by accumulation, one card at a time, and it is most of why no single hand gets ahead.

Nothing is foil and nothing is borderless. Nine legendary frames, three enchantment frames, one spree. This is a working deck, sleeved at working prices, and it looks like one on purpose.

also_worth_noting.note: Exquisite Blood and Beseech the Mirror — the fastest kill's scarce half, and the wish that misses it by one: the bargain stops at four and the Blood costs five.
Butcher Ghoul and Supernatural Stamina — a body that dies twice on its own, and the trick that makes any body die twice.
Animate Dead and Ashnod's Altar — the reanimation spell and the free outlet, both still doing precisely what they did when they were printed.
Stitcher's Supplier and The Meathook Massacre — the one-drop that fills your graveyard, and the wipe that bills the table while it empties the board.
Cabal Pit and Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth — two lands from one hand, both older than half the pod and both still earning the slot.

rhythm_notes: Act I opens on instruction (The Command Zone: one hero image, the tax ladder, the phase rule), climbs to the issue's narrative high in The Game Plan, then drops to the lowest-effort spread in the book — The 99, eleven roster groups you browse rather than read. Act II climbs again: practice in Keep or Ship, two participation spreads in What's Your Play?, then The Kill as the mid-book peak carrying the heaviest furniture in the issue — eight callout-steps for six shapes and their bounds — exactly where the reader has the most momentum. Act III runs single-voice and medium the whole way: reflection (Table Manners), reference (Know Your Enemy's six threat boxes), instruction (Fetch Quests) — the deliberate long exhale after the peak. Act IV carries the issue's only dense adjacency, Sources Say into By the Numbers, and it is legal because the renderer emits the declared full-bleed art break between them; The Short List then drops to imagination as the trough before the appendix. Act V descends cleanly: Judge's Desk is opt-in deep reference with one component and no callouts, Featured Artist is the palate cleanser with a breadth story instead of a manufactured star, the Back Page closes. Furniture is thinnest where intensity is lowest — Judge's Desk carries a pull quote and nothing else; The Short List one caption and no tips.
gaps: IDENTITY GATE FOR THE ORCHESTRATOR: issue.json stamps decklist_sha256 7eef02f1... while cards.json carries 3ddfb869... — validate-issue will fail the identity check until the stamped hash is deliberately updated to the decklist this issue actually describes.

PRESENTATION GATE: fourteen stacks are checker-passed and eleven are presentable; files 001, 007 and 013 resolve boards holding Blowfly Infestation or Necroskitter, which are not in the 99, so every count in this plan — eleven files, eight kill files, six shapes — is written against the eleven. The proliferate token-count arithmetic (three Insects, not six) is echoed only as settled prose, with no file number attached.

DECISION 002's own title states a kill count in its own words that predates the six-shape taxonomy; the What's Your Play? furniture deliberately quotes no kill count so the page cannot contradict itself, but a scoped revision of that decision title would remove the tension entirely.

STACK 014 SETTLES the diagnosis's first open question — the undying pair now has a checker-passed artifact — so the diagnosis's hedged SPOF language about Mikaeus can be un-hedged at its next regeneration.

STACK SCENARIOS WORTH SPAWNING, RANKED: (1) the six shapes under a resolved Grafdigger's Cage — four of six look Cage-shaped on oracle reading, most of this issue's political advice rests on it, and nothing signed settles it; (2) the outlet class under Cursed Totem — whether any kill assembles through the noncreature remainder decides how deep the artifact hole goes; (3) The Meathook Massacre as a substitute drain in the recursion loops, which would widen the slot three signed kills share; (4) Exquisite Blood ignition via Marauding Blight-Priest or Starscape Cleric, since neither gains life by itself and the signed board ignited from the Avatar's own dies-trigger; (5) the bare Mikaeus two-card records — eight of the eleven bracket-forcing infinites are in that family, none has counter-stripping on plain reading, and the strategic frame flags them as the containment block most likely to be refuted.

FEATURED ARTIST IS THIN AND HONEST: no standout exists (deepest credit three cards), so the section runs as a breadth feature; the note states the per-entry counting rule, names the 21-copy Swamp trap, and claims no curation the analysis cannot support (drop_runs is empty).

STRATEGY DB HOLES THIS ISSUE WROTE AROUND (from the frame's gap list): no aristocrats outlet/fodder/payoff section; no vocabulary for what BOUNDS an iterative engine — this issue ships one of each kind; no theory of creation-side versus death-side trigger surface (file 008's finding); nothing pricing a recursive copy above a one-shot in redundancy math; no class for mana-free self-funding kills, this deck's best property under tax; no discipline for reading six correlated kill rates as one number — By the Numbers declines instead; and no guidance for a SPLIT kill suite's commander insurance, which The Command Zone coaches as protect-by-phase.

TIER DISCIPLINE: the six shapes are stated as fact only with their file numbers; every assembly percentage is phrased as a draw rate, never a win rate; the 39 contained lines and eleven two-card records are named as containment, never evidence; The Command Zone fences its judgment under COACH'S READ. PUN BUDGET: three, all in furniture — 'THE HUB IN FURNITURE'S CLOTHES', 'THE COST THAT ISN'T', and the headline 'SIXTY-EIGHT HANDS, NO HEADLINER'.
